conclusion.justification: The report explicitly concludes that hydroxychloroquine does not reduce mortality from COVID-19, citing large randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses showing no mortality benefit and potential harm.
conclusion.label: rejects

report:
# Conclusion

No, hydroxychloroquine does not reduce mortality from COVID-19. The strongest available evidence—large randomized controlled trials—consistently shows no mortality benefit, and some data suggest possible harm.

The UK RECOVERY trial, one of the largest randomized platform trials for COVID-19 treatments, found that hydroxychloroquine was not associated with reduced mortality in hospitalized patients compared to usual care, leading investigators to conclude "hydroxychloroquine does not reduce the risk of death among hospitalised patients with COVID-19" (https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa2022926). This result was significant enough that the trial's hydroxychloroquine arm was halted early.

Similarly, the WHO Solidarity Trial—a multinational randomized trial—found that hydroxychloroquine produced "little or no reduction in the mortality of hospitalised COVID-19 patients when compared to standard of care," prompting WHO to halt this treatment arm (https://www.aljazeera.com/news/2020/7/4/who-halts-hydroxychloroquine-in-covid-19-trials-live-updates).

A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examining hydroxychloroquine's effects on mortality, viral clearance, and other outcomes in COVID-19 patients corroborated these findings, showing no mortality benefit (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8013604/).

Additionally, a separate meta-analysis published in Nature Communications reported that hydroxychloroquine/chloroquine treatment was actually associated with **increased mortality** in COVID-19 patients across combined trial data (https://www.nature.com/articles/s41467-021-22446-z).

Based on this body of high-quality randomized trial evidence, hydroxychloroquine should not be used to reduce COVID-19 mortality risk, and regulatory bodies including the WHO have discontinued its use in COVID-19 treatment protocols based on these findings.
